name: Back-rank mate
goal: You can mate a king trapped behind its own pawns on the back rank, and give your own king an escape square in time.

intro.text: A king tucked behind its own pawns is safe from most attacks, but those same pawns can trap it. If an enemy rook or queen reaches the king's first rank with check, the king has nowhere to go, and it is mate. This back-rank mate decides many games at every level. You will learn to give it, to deal with the piece that guards against it, and to give your own king a way out before it is too late.

parts.title: Mate on the back rank
parts.keyIdea: A rook or queen that checks along the first rank mates a king whose own pawns block its way out.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. Black has just taken your rook on d3 and is a rook ahead. But that rook has left Black's back rank, and the king on g8 is walled in by its own pawns.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: Your rook checks along the eighth rank. The king cannot step up, because its own pawns stand on f7, g7 and h7. Black's only way out of check is to block with the rook: 32...Rd8.
Take the rook that blocked. It is check again, nothing is left to block with, and the king still cannot move: back-rank mate.

parts.title: Take the guard
parts.keyIdea: If a single piece guards the square where you would mate, take that piece, even if it costs your queen.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. White's rook has just dropped back to c1, where it attacks your queen. Your rook on e8 would mate on e1 if nothing guarded that square. What guards it?

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: Give up your queen for the rook. It is check, so White has to answer it, and the rook on c1 was the only piece guarding e1.
White's bishop took back on c1, so nothing guards e1 any more. Your rook checks along the first rank, and the pawns on f2, g2 and h2 keep the king in: mate.

parts.title: One guard, two jobs
parts.keyIdea: A piece that guards the back rank cannot also guard something else; attack the other thing and the back rank opens.
parts.text: From the game Bernstein–Capablanca, Moscow 1914, with you playing Black. Only White's queen on e2 stops your rook from landing on d1, and White's rook on c3 has no protection at all.

notes.text: Your queen attacks the rook on c3 and White's queen at the same time. White cannot take your queen: 30.Qxb2 would leave d1 unguarded, and 30...Rd1 is mate.
30.Qe1 protects the rook and still guards the first rank, so the queen now has two jobs. Take the rook: if White takes back, the back rank is left without a guard.
31.Qxc3 was a mistake, because the queen has left the first rank. Your rook checks on d1, and White's only defence is to block with the queen: 32.Qe1.
Take the queen with check. The king on g1 is shut in by its own pawns: back-rank mate.

parts.title: Give your king air
parts.keyIdea: Before the back rank becomes a trap, move a pawn in front of your king so that it has a square to escape to.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. Black's queen and rook are lined up on the f-file, and your king cannot leave the first rank: g2 and h2 hold its own pawns, and Black's queen covers f2. In the game White played 23.Qe4 and allowed a mate in three; find a move that ends the danger for good.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: Black was threatening 23...Qf2+ 24.Kh1 Qf1+ 25.Rxf1 Rxf1, mate on the back rank. The pawn move gives your king the h2 square, so that mate no longer works.
The king steps into the square the pawn made for it. It is safe on h2, and you are two pawns ahead.
